paper_title: Supervising the Visible State: Separating Representation from View Selection in Streaming Video

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: An action seen once and the same action seen three times receive the same action-recognition label, so that supervision does not require a model to count. Answers shared across histories that differ in event order, accumulation, or relations leave those distinctions unconstrained; we call this state under-specification. Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) addresses it by training on source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency; under the same recent-frame interface it improves OVO-Bench over a strict-matched generic temporal supervision baseline while remaining comparable on StreamingBench, with the largest gain in hallucination detection. Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) then adapts evidence access while keeping the learned model fixed, expanding from recent frames to sparse event and compact history views on demand. The two interventions separate representation from view selection: supervision particularly benefits hallucination detection and causal reasoning, access particularly benefits event recall and forward reasoning. Together they reach the best reported accuracy among the published systems compared here on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench at a fraction of the processed frames of exhaustive selection, and strict replay shows that most of the remaining gap to a three-view oracle is a correct answer that was later replaced. Streaming accuracy depends on what supervision asks the model to keep, what evidence inference exposes, and whether the model keeps a correct answer once it has one.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Picture an assistant that watches through camera glasses. Midway through workout it is asked, How many push-ups was that? Its current frame shows person at the top of push-up; whether that was the fifth or the fifteenth is not in the frame. In the kitchen, Did the garlic go in before the onions? and Did turn the stove off? are questions of the same kind, and if the stove was never in view, the honest answer is that it cannot tell. This is the streaming setting: at time , model answers from the observed prefix VT under bounded context and computation [4, 35], without the complete recording that offline models [2, 8, 9, 22, 62] and their benchmarks [13, 32, 65] assume. What it can answer depends on what it has retained about the history, not only on what it currently sees. The push-up question already shows what that retention must contain. Two histories that end with the same movement, one after single repetition and one after three, receive the same action label; only counting question separates them. The same holds for the order of events and for the object relations they leave behind. We call the temporal content that bounded causal view establishes its visible state: which events occurred, in what order, how often, which relations changed, and whether the evidence suffices to answer at all. ❶ Answer-level supervision under-specifies this state: an answer shared across temporally different histories leaves those distinctions unconstrained, so nothing in the target 1 requires the model to keep count, order, or relations. We call this supervision-level ambiguity state under-specification; temporal benchmarks show that exactly these distinctions are where video LLMs remain weak [3, 29, 37, 61]. Related work on sequential state tracking makes intermediate progress explicit by aligning recurrent predictions with operationprefix states [44], connecting the supervision target to the distinctions needed during computation. Most streaming methods are context-centric: they organize the growing visual context, through token compression [24, 39, 41, 57], persistent memories [17, 19, 50, 59, 60], or event-based retrieval [11, 14, 43, 52], and thereby decide which evidence stays accessible; our focus is how the supervision formulation shapes what the model can infer from that evidence. SimpleStream [38] shows that an off-the-shelf VLM reading few recent causal frames already matches far more elaborate systems. Yet ❷ representation, however stateful, can ground only the observations its view exposes: with four recent frames, the history that recall and counting questions need is absent (Figure 1). Representation and view selection are therefore two separable levers, and we measure each with controlled intervention on one backbone, Qwen3-VL-8B with the latest four frames. In this paper, we move both levers. First, due to ❶, we design Visible-State Supervision (ViSS), which trains on probes whose targets require the missing distinctions; the 7,677-example mixture is grounded in source annotations or frames and trains in one epoch. Under the same recent-4 interface it improves both benchmarks, and strict-matched generic temporal SFT control shows that the visible-state formulation adds to the OVO-Bench gain from temporal post-training (Section 5.3). Sufficiency is part of this state: removing examples whose answer is that the evidence does not suffice is associated with lower hallucination-detection accuracy. Second, to address ❷, we introduce Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS), which freezes the ViSS checkpoint and changes only the view, cascading from the recent view to sparse event view when the recent answer is uncertain and to compact history view when the two disagree. With the checkpoint frozen it adds further gains on both benchmarks at third to half of the frames of exhaustive three-view selection (Section 5.3). Together the two levers reach 86.33 on StreamingBench and 69.77 on OVO-Bench, +5.81 and +10.80 points over the same backbone (Figure 3); strict replay attributes most of the remaining gap to three-view oracle to correct answer that was held and then replaced. Our contributions are: We identify state under-specification in answer-level supervision and address it with ViSS, 7,677 source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and sufficiency. At matched backbone and budget, it exceeds strict-matched generic temporal SFT by +1.73 points on OVO-Bench and +8.06 points on hallucination detection. We distinguish supervision and evidence access through matched-training and fixed-checkpoint comparisons. Supervision mainly improves hallucination detection and causal reasoning; access, through TVS, mainly improves event recall and forward reasoning at fraction of the frames of exhaustive selection. Strict replay attributes 66.9% and 71.9% of the remaining oracle gap to replacing an already correct answer, identifying commitment stability as the main selection limitation within this subset.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Streaming post-training. Prior work adapts multimodal models to causal observation through causal temporal attention [55], large-scale multitask instructions [54], supervised visual clues and response states [23], streaming interaction formats [5, 27, 49], reasoning that evolves with the stream [16, 30] or is reinforced with rule-based rewards [12], and selfgenerated causal trajectories [53]. Counting benchmarks also probe streaming state maintenance [28]. In audio-visual reasoning, OmniVideo-R1 combines query-intensive grounding and modality-attentive fusion within reinforcementlearning framework [7]. We complement these directions by separating temporal post-training, visible-state formulation, and evidence access. In this work, we target the unconstrained temporal distinctions with source-grounded probes under fixed recent-4 view; the trade-off is that no architectural state is added, so the model can only ground what its view exposes. View selection. Streaming systems bound what the model sees by compressing visual tokens or KV caches [24, 39, 41, 57], maintaining external or recurrent memories [17, 34, 50, 59, 60], retrieving cached context [10], organizing history through event-aware or query-addressable structures [11, 14, 43, 52], selecting frames [42, 58], or acting as 2 Figure 1: Context-centric streaming versus supervising the visible state. Top: recent-frame models see little history and history-centric models leave temporal composition implicit; both inherit answer-level supervision, whereas we supervise the visible state and acquire causal views on demand. Bottom: counting movie inserts, the recent view misses earlier ones and historical sampling skips the first; retrieving it restores the count. This example does not separate the two levers. agents that decide what to inspect [47, 51, 56, 63]. AtlasVA organizes reusable visual skills through spatial heatmaps, visual exemplars, and symbolic text skills [45]. SimpleStream [38] shows that few recent frames already form strong reference and motivates accessing history on demand (Figure 1). In this work, TVS makes that direction concrete as fixed family of three causal views with calibrated acquisition and commitment on the frozen ViSS checkpoint; the trade-off is query-independent view family rather than learned retrieval, which lets its effect be measured separately from supervision.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: ViSS first trains shared parameters on temporally structured targets; TVS then freezes them and varies the evidence presented at inference (Figure 2). Evaluating the checkpoint under recent-4 access before enabling TVS yields the two contrasts in Eq. 2.

sections.title: 4.1 Visible-State Supervision
sections.content: Motivation. By ❶, an answer-level target leaves multiplicity, order, relations, and sufficiency unconstrained. The remedy is to ask for them directly: when targets are determined by the supplied view, separating probe requires loss-minimizing representation to keep the distinction (Proposition 1, Appendix F), and asking for several jointly makes the requirements complementary rather than task-specific. Probe families. Each probe pairs causal training view xi with question requesting one temporal readout: identity probes ask which events occurred, order probes their sequence, accumulation probes the quantities established by the prefix, relation probes how observed states changed, and sufficiency probes whether the supplied evidence supports determinate answer, in the spirit of unanswerable questions [36]. Every family uses the shared computation in Eq. 1, with direct option, binary value, or integer as the target. An identity target can be satisfied without recovering an events multiplicity or position; counting and ordering targets make those distinctions necessary, and sufficiency targets penalize commitment when the evidence is inadequate. Fixed-view evaluation then tests whether the joint requirement transfers to temporal decisions under bounded views. Source-grounded construction. We construct probes directly from source annotations whenever the required event, timestamp, or relation is available; for capabilities absent from the annotations, teacher proposes candidate question answer pairs from source pixels, timestamps, and family-specific instruction, as in synthetic video instruction data [6, 31, 64], behind construction firewall that excludes benchmark media, questions, answers, task metadata, student predictions, and evaluation feedback. sections.title: 4.2 Test-Time Causal View Search
sections.content: Motivation. By ❷, even the ViSS representation can ground only what its view exposes, and recent-4 omits the history that recall and counting need. Exposing the full history at every query is costly and often unnecessary, so inference compute should go where it helps [40], and the models own confidence signals when more evidence is needed [20, 21]. TVS therefore expands the view on demand with the checkpoint frozen. Causal views. Let gk denote question-independent operator that renders the prefix as xe,k = gk(Pe(Te)); each view is processed by the same representation and readout in Eq. 1 with θ frozen. The recent view g0 keeps the latest four frames at full detail; the event view g1 adds up to 16 earlier frames ranked by visual change; the compact-history view g2 exposes broader portion of the prefix at reduced resolution while keeping high-resolution recent evidence. All three share the causal endpoint Te, preserve chronological order, and are independent of the question, options, and task type; each call exposes at most 32 frames, and three-call path processes at most 56 frames including repeats (Appendix A). Acquisition. What if the recent view is not enough? Each call returns an answer ˆye,k and confidence margin me,k, the difference between the two largest full-vocabulary probabilities at the first answer position. TVS starts from the recent view and expands only when the current prediction warrants it: recent-view margin below τa activates the event view, and disagreement between the recent and event proposals activates compact history. Commitment. What if later view is wrong? Acquiring evidence and revising the answer are separate decisions, and unlike voting over sampled answers [48], proposals are compared by margin across views. disagreeing proposal replaces the retained proposal only when me,k me,j > τc; because the calibrated τc is negative, an accepted proposal need not have higher raw margin than the retained answer. Both thresholds are calibrated once on sourcevideo-disjoint holdout and fixed across benchmarks; exact rules, pseudocode, causality audits, and frame accounting are in Appendix A; Appendix analyzes the gate and the sign of τc.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We organize the analysis around four questions. RQ1: does supervising visible-state distinctions help beyond generic temporal post-training at the same budget, and where is the additional gain concentrated? RQ2: what does view selection add on frozen checkpoint, and at what frame cost (both in Sections 5.2 and 5.3)? RQ3: do supervision and access improve the same tasks (Section 5.2)? RQ4: when TVS still fails, is the correct answer unavailable or lost (Section 5.4)?

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate on StreamingBench [25] (2,495 queries) and OVO-Bench (3,035 queries) using the full splits, the official scorers, and the same recent-4 starting view; StreamingBench uses letter-exact accuracy, and OVO-Bench averages task accuracies within its real-time, backward, and forward groups, then the three groups. Published systems in Tables 1 and 2 keep their own protocols (Appendix C.4); our claims rest on the controlled rows, which share one backbone, scorer, and starting view. Within them, representation comparisons vary the checkpoint under fixed recent-4 access, and access comparisons freeze the ViSS checkpoint and vary only the view policy; no policy uses benchmark task labels or task-specific routing. The backbone is Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [1]: ViSS is fresh one-epoch SFT run with frozen vision tower, taking 98 minutes on two H100 GPUs, and TVS starts from the same recent-4 input, makes at most three calls, and exposes at most 32 causal frames per call, with thresholds fixed on source-disjoint holdout. Data construction and full configurations are in Appendices and B.3.

sections.title: 5.2 Comparison Experiments
sections.content: The recent-4 baseline is already strong: Qwen3-VL-8B with four recent frames scores 80.52 and 58.97, above most published systems in Tables 1 and 2, including ones that maintain persistent memories or retrieve events [38], so every gain below is measured against competitive starting point on the same backbone. Both interventions then add on both benchmarks: the complete ViSS post-training recipe raises the recent-4 scores by +4.25 and +6.24 after one epoch on 7,677 examples, and TVS adds +1.56 and +4.56 with the checkpoint frozen and at most three calls per query. The complete system reaches 86.33 and 69.77, +5.81 and +10.80 points above the same backbone. These are the highest reported scores among the listed systems under their respective protocols, and the two interventions improve different tasks. OVO-Bench. Table 1 and Figure 3(a) show that supervision and access improve different tasks. Under the same recent-4 interface, the full post-training recipe adds +6.24 points, and most of the Backward gain is hallucination detection, known weakness of vision-language models [15]: HLD doubles from 37.63 to 75.27, whereas EPM moves from 54.55 to 57.24 and ASI from 62.16 to 60.14. Against strict-matched generic supervision, HLD rises from 67.20 to 75.27; transfer across the other temporal tasks is smaller and heterogeneous. Knowing that the visible evidence does not answer the question is part of the visible state, and the sufficiency-removal comparison in Section 5.3 shows concentrated decline in hallucination detection. Forward reasoning also improves under fixed views (SSR +7.8, CRR +6.3). Freezing the checkpoint and enabling TVS adds another +4.56 points with the opposite profile: EPM rises to 68.35 and ASI to 68.24, REC nearly doubles from 21.20 to 39.83, and CRR rises to 62.08, while HLD falls to 71.51 and the real-time average slips from 82.20 to 81.27. The slip is consistent with the imperfect preservation of correct recent answers measured in Section 5.4. In short, broader evidence buys recall and forward reasoning at small cost in hallucination detection and real-time perception (RQ3). StreamingBench. Table 2 shows the same division. When correct proposal is available, TVS returns it in 63.3% and 71.1% of cases, and it preserves an initially correct recent answer in 96.9% and 92.3%. The three-view oracle, which uses the reference answer to pick correct proposal whenever any view produces one, reaches 91.42 and 78.52, 5.09 and 8.75 points above TVS. Trace-level attribution over the 127 and 270 gap queries assigns 66.9% and 71.9% of them to replacement errors, in which correct proposal was retained and then replaced by later view (Figure 3(c)); acquisition misses account for most of the remainder, and outright rejection of correct proposal is rare. Within these oracle-gap cases, retaining an available correct answer is the dominant selection limitation. This diagnosis is conditional on proposal coverage; it does not account for all-view unresolved errors or establish benefit of the current margin rule (RQ4; Appendices and A.3). Related work studies selective correction through diagnosis-guided recovery [46] and the reliability of retaining intermediate results across reasoning attempts [26]. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Streaming accuracy depends on three separable factors: what the supervision asks the model to preserve, what evidence inference exposes, and whether the model keeps correct answer once it has one. Visible-state supervision adds to matched temporal post-training, particularly in hallucination detection; causal view search addresses the second, above all event recall and forward reasoning. Within the gap to the current three-view oracle, replacing retained correct answer is the dominant selection error, motivating more stable answer selection. The controlled study uses one 8B backbone and two benchmarks; cross-scale and cross-family transfer remain open. Gains vary across tasks: supervision particularly benefits state fidelity, while adaptive access improves recall and forward reasoning at cost on some recent-state decisions.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: Generative AI was used in two roles. During data construction, multimodal teacher proposed candidate question answer pairs and linguistic variants from source video frames, timestamps, and generation instructions. It had no access to evaluation questions, reference answers, task metadata, or student predictions; its outputs entered training only after deterministic semantic, causal, source-membership, and overlap checks. These checks do not certify that every target requires historical evidence. AI assistants also supported code editing, literature search, and manuscript revision. The authors designed the research, verified all code, citations, claims, and reported numbers against source papers and versioned result records, and take responsibility for the complete work.

sections.title: Ethics statement
sections.content: This work uses existing research video datasets and public benchmarks; it recruits no human participants and collects no new video. Videos may contain identifiable people or contextual information, so any release follows the source licenses and does not redistribute benchmark media. Benchmark examples and labels are excluded from training, and benchmark identity and task type are not available to the data compiler or TVS policy. Continuous video understanding can nevertheless enable surveillance and inherit social or demographic biases that we have not audited. We therefore do not claim suitability for surveillance or other high-stakes deployment.

sections.title: Reproducibility statement
sections.content: Appendices and B.3 specify the data pipeline, 7,677-example training mixture, model initialization, optimization, and evaluation protocols. Every retained SFT comparison is fresh run from the same public checkpoint; TVS keeps the ViSS checkpoint and its holdout-calibrated thresholds fixed. Model weights, processors, source code, and example configurations are available through the ViSS resource collection. Training annotations, raw media, and internal experiment records are not included in this release. The view compiler excludes question and answer content; timestamp and strict-replay checks are scoped in Appendix A.3. All reported values are defined once in numbers.tex and traced to versioned result records.

sections.title: A Causal Views and Adaptive View Selection
sections.content: This appendix specifies how complementary observations of one causal prefix are constructed and sequentially consulted by TVS. For query qe issued at time te, every view is compiled from Vte independently of the query and answer content. All policies use the same frozen ViSS checkpoint θ, greedy decoding, and the shared fixed configuration recorded below. A.1 Complementary Causal Views The recent view xe,0 preserves local detail at the query frontier; the event view xe,1 adds sparse transitions from earlier in the prefix; and the compact-history view xe,2 trades historical spatial resolution for greater temporal coverage. Table 4 defines these observation operators. They share causal endpoint, not an identical frame grid: event and compact-history views are compiled separately and are not strictly nested. sections.content: This appendix makes the two levers precise. Proposition 1 formalizes state under-specification (❶) and shows what separating probe adds to an answer-level objective. Proposition 2 shows that for Bayes-optimal readout wider causal view never loses accuracy and no commitment rule can beat it. The replacement errors in Section 5.4 concern the deployed readout and selection policy within fixed proposal set. Propositions 3 and 4 give conditions under which the margin gate of TVS is the optimal acquisition rule and explain why its calibrated commit threshold is negative. All statements concern population quantities and unrestricted predictor classes: they describe what the objectives and decision rules can and cannot enforce, not finite-sample behavior. The semantic-stability check of Section 4.1 tests invariance to option permutation; it does not establish the view-consistency assumption or human unambiguity of target. Proposition 2 separates two readings of the replacement errors in Section 5.4. For Bayes readout on the wider view, replacing the retained answer can still be wrong on individual queries, but no rule that keeps the retained answer more often can raise accuracy. The deployed readout need not be Bayes-optimal, so this result does not imply that proposal selection cannot improve its accuracy. The three-view oracle uses reference answers and is not Bayes-risk estimate; its gap diagnoses selection failures within the current proposal set. The commit-margin ablation in Section 5.3 evaluates one particular selection rule, not the potential of all commitment rules. Suppose disagreeing proposals (retained) and (new) have correctness probabilities that depend on the margins only through view-specific increasing calibration maps, (j correct mj, mk) = φj(mj) and (k correct mj, mk) = φk(mk). The accuracy-maximizing commitment rule takes iff φk(mk) > φj(mj). If the two maps differ by shift, φk(m) = φj(m + δ), this rule reads mk mj > δ, which is the TVS rule with τc = δ. Proof. Given the margins, keeping is correct with probability φj(mj) and taking with probability φk(mk), so picking the larger probability maximizes expected accuracy pointwise. Under the shift, φk(mk) > φj(mj) iff φj(mk + δ) > φj(mj) iff mk + δ > mj, because φj is increasing. negative calibrated τc (Section 4.2) is thus what one expects when wider views yield lower raw margins at equal accuracy, as happens when more frames spread probability over more plausible answers; the holdout calibration estimates δ without modeling φj explicitly. Proposition 2 adds the caveat that, for Bayes readout on the wider view, the best value of this rule is to always accept, so any accuracy the rule adds in practice is symptom of readout miscalibration that it partially corrects.
